subject: A heart attack
object: blood flow to the heart is blocked; it can be life-threatening and needs emergency hospital treatment.
source_quote: A heart attack happens when blood flow to your heart is blocked. It can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

subject: Heart attack symptoms
object: crushing or squeezing chest pain that may spread to the arm, neck or jaw; breathlessness; nausea or vomiting; indigestion with chest burning or feeling full or bloated; sweating; and pale, blue or grey skin, which may be easier to see on the palms in black or brown skin.
source_quote: Symptoms of a heart attack may include: chest pain which may feel like crushing or squeezing on your chest – the pain may also spread to your arm, neck and jaw feeling short of breath feeling sick (nausea) or being sick (vomiting) feeling like you have indigestion – you may have a burning feeling in your chest and feel full or bloated sweating pale, blue or grey skin – on black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands

subject: A heart attack
object: a blood clot preventing enough blood from reaching the heart.
source_quote: Heart attacks are usually caused by a blood clot stopping enough blood getting to your heart.

subject: Myocardial infarction
object: myocardial cell death due to prolonged myocardial ischaemia, meaning inadequate oxygen supply to the myocardium.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: Myocardial infarction (MI) is defined pathologically as myocardial cell death attributable to prolonged myocardial ischemia (inadequate oxygen supply to the myocardium).

subject: Type 1 myocardial infarction
object: a primary coronary arterial event caused by atherothrombotic plaque rupture or erosion.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: Type 1 MI is a primary coronary arterial event attributable to atherothrombotic plaque rupture or erosion.

subject: Type 2 myocardial infarction
object: an acute myocardial oxygen supply-demand imbalance without atherothrombosis: reduced perfusion may occur with fixed coronary atherosclerosis without plaque disruption, coronary spasm, microvascular dysfunction, embolism, dissection, hypoxaemia, anaemia, hypotension or bradyarrhythmia, while tachyarrhythmia or severe hypertension may increase oxygen demand.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: Type 2 MI occurs secondary to an acute imbalance in myocardial oxygen supply and demand without atherothrombosis. This imbalance may be attributable to reduced myocardial perfusion in the context of fixed coronary atherosclerosis (without plaque disruption), coronary artery spasm, microvascular dysfunction, coronary embolism, dissection, or systemic causes such as hypoxemia, anemia, hypotension, or bradyarrhythmia, or increased myocardial oxygen demand attributable to tachyarrhythmia or severe hypertension.

subject: Myocardial injury
object: acute injury shows dynamic cardiac troponin changes on serial measurements, whereas chronic injury shows stable or minimally changing concentrations on serial measurements.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: Myocardial injury may be acute, manifested as dynamic changes in cTn concentration over serial measurements, or chronic, in which concentrations are stable or change minimally over serial measurement (Figure 1).

subject: In acute myocardial injury, a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction
object: myocardial-ischaemia symptoms, ischaemic ECG signs such as ST-segment changes or pathological Q waves, or evidence of a new regional wall-motion abnormality.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: Among patients with acute myocardial injury in whom there are symptoms of myocardial ischemia, signs of ischemia on the ECG (ST-segment changes or the development of pathological Q waves), or evidence of a new regional wall motion abnormality, the diagnosis of acute MI is applied.

subject: Symptoms associated with myocardial ischaemia
object: chest, upper-limb, mandibular or epigastric discomfort and dyspnoea or fatigue during exertion or at rest; regardless of duration these symptoms are not specific for myocardial ischaemia, and myocardial infarction may have atypical symptoms or no symptoms at all.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: The UDMI notes the following symptoms, in various combinations, as associated with myocardial ischemia: chest, upper extremity, mandibular, or epigastric discomfort, and dyspnea or fatigue during exertion or at rest. However, these symptoms, regardless of duration, are not specific for myocardial ischemia, and MI may occur with atypical symptoms or even without symptoms at all.

subject: Symptoms atypical for myocardial ischaemia
object: people with diabetes, older people and women, who together account for the majority ultimately diagnosed with acute myocardial infarction; surveillance studies found up to 45% of all myocardial infarctions to be silent or unrecognised, with mortality similar to recognised infarctions.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: Symptoms atypical for myocardial ischemia are more common in diabetic patients, the elderly, and women, a combined demographic that accounts for the majority of patients ultimately diagnosed with acute MI. – Moreover, surveillance studies have found up to 45% of all MIs to be silent or unrecognized with mortality rates similar to recognized MIs.,

subject: Dynamic ST-segment changes
object: only a minority of people with myocardial infarction and cannot reliably distinguish type 1 from type 2 myocardial infarction.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: However, dynamic ST-segment changes are found in only a minority of patients with MI, and cannot reliably discriminate type 1 from type 2 MI (Table II in the online-only Data Supplement).

subject: Baseline or peak cardiac troponin levels
relation: cannot accurately distinguish myocardial-injury aetiologies because
object: their ranges overlap, despite significant differences in distributions in several studies.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: Although significant differences in the distribution of baseline or peak cTn levels are evident in several studies, overlapping ranges limit the use of cTn levels to accurately differentiate between etiologies of myocardial injury (Figure 3).

subject: To find out if someone is having a heart attack, they
object: tests including an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests.
source_quote: How a heart attack is diagnosed You'll need tests including an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests to find out if you're having a heart attack.

subject: If initial tests show a heart attack, further tests
object: an echocardiogram to check heart damage or a coronary angiogram to find exactly where blood flow is blocked, with the blockage possibly treated at the same time; a doctor will discuss what the results may mean.
source_quote: If these tests show you're having a heart attack, you may have further tests such as: an echocardiogram, which can find out if your heart has been damaged a coronary angiogram, which can find out exactly where the blood flow to your heart is blocked – the blockage may be treated at the same time A doctor will discuss what your test results may mean for you.

subject: The NHS emergency advice for a possible heart attack
object: tight or squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to the arms or neck or jaw, severe breathing difficulty with gasping or choking or inability to speak, pale or blue or grey lips or skin that may be easier to see on the palms in brown or black skin, or someone who has passed out and is not responding normally; do not drive yourself to A&E, and the person answering 999 will advise what to do.
source_quote: Heart attack Immediate action required: Call 999 if: you have chest pain that feels tight or like squeezing on your chest you have chest pain that's spreading to your arms, neck or jaw you're having severe difficulty breathing – you're gasping, choking or not able to get words out your lips or skin are pale, blue or grey – on brown or black skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands someone has passed out and is not responding normally Do not drive yourself to A&E. The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

subject: If you think you or someone else is having a heart attack, while waiting for help,
object: comfortably on the floor with knees bent and back supported, or on a chair if that is not possible; take aspirin (300mg) if available but do not give it to someone allergic to aspirin; if you have angina, take your GTN spray if you have it; keep checking the person is responding and breathing, and start CPR if they stop responding and stop breathing.
source_quote: If you think you or someone else is having a heart attack, there are some things you can do while you wait for help. Sit and rest on the floor in a comfortable position, with your knees bent and your back supported. If you cannot do this, you can also sit on a chair. Take aspirin (300mg) if you have any – do not give aspirin to someone who has an aspirin allergy. If you have angina, take your glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray if you have it with you. Keep checking someone who may be having a heart attack to make sure they're still responding and breathing. If someone stops responding to you and stops breathing, start CPR.

subject: A heart attack
relation: needs hospital treatment depending on severity, which may include
object: medicines to treat the arterial blockage and improve blood flow, coronary angioplasty using a small plastic tube called a stent to open blocked arteries, or coronary bypass surgery using arteries from elsewhere in the body to take blood around the blockage.
source_quote: You'll need treatment in hospital for a heart attack. Your treatment will depend on how severe it is. Treatments may include: medicines to treat the blockage in your arteries and improve blood flow to your heart a procedure to improve blood flow to your heart (coronary angioplasty) – this involves opening blocked arteries using a small plastic tube called a stent surgery where arteries are taken from another part of your body and used in your heart to take blood around a blocked artery (coronary artery bypass)

subject: After a heart attack, long-term medicines
object: to treat its causes and help reduce the risk of another heart attack; they may include antiplatelets to help stop arterial blockage, statins to lower cholesterol and high-blood-pressure medicines such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers.
source_quote: You will be given medicines to take long-term after having a heart attack. They treat the causes of your heart attack and help reduce your risk of having another one. These medicines may include: antiplatelets to help stop your arteries getting blocked statins to lower your cholesterol other medicines to lower high blood pressure, such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers

subject: After a heart attack, people
object: rest, including time off work, and referral to cardiac rehabilitation for recovery, which may be delivered in person or remotely using video calls or apps.
source_quote: After having a heart attack, you'll usually: need to rest, including taking time off work be referred to cardiac rehabilitation to help with your recovery – this may involve attending appointments in-person, or taking part remotely from home using video calls or apps

subject: A heart attack
object: people who smoke, have high blood pressure or high cholesterol, have a close relative who has had a heart attack, have diabetes, or live with overweight or obesity.
source_quote: You're more likely to have a heart attack if you: smoke have high blood pressure have high cholesterol have a close relative who's had a heart attack have diabetes are living with overweight or obesity

subject: A heart attack
relation: is life-threatening and cannot always be treated;
object: there is a chance the affected person may die.
source_quote: A heart attack is a life-threatening condition and cannot always be treated. There's a chance someone who has one may die.

subject: Chronic myocardial injury
object: persistently elevated cardiac troponin without the dynamic rise or fall of acute myocardial infarction or acute nonischaemic injury; structural abnormalities such as left ventricular hypertrophy or dysfunction and noncardiac conditions such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease may contribute.
source: Article: DeFilippis AP, Chapman AR, Mills NL et al. Assessment and Treatment of Patients With Type 2 Myocardial Infarction and Acute Nonischemic Myocardial Injury. Circulation 2019
source_quote: Persistently elevated cTn levels that do not demonstrate a dynamic rising and/or falling pattern as seen in acute MI or acute nonischemic myocardial injury are categorized as chronic myocardial injury. Both structural cardiac abnormalities (eg, left ventricular hypertrophy, left ventricular dysfunction) and noncardiac conditions (eg, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease) may contribute to chronic myocardial injury.
